rv.q: Smart elevates the material and makes Izzy's story feel fresh, authentic and always compelling.
It’s a terrific performance, but one that nevertheless remains constrained by the material’s limitations.
Returning to Broadway after 25 years in “Call Me Izzy,” which opened Thursday at Studio 54, Jean Smart crushes it in the good way.

Skinner’s dissection of the red-pilled male mind-set does not seem particularly sharp to me: she is deft at showing how a “just asking questions” manner actually masks deep resentment, but she’s less careful with the specifics.
It's easy to cheer for Smart, and as evidenced by rounds of pitying applause at Studio 54, a little too easy for this show.
So, why, why, why has she chosen to return to Broadway in the anemic, copy-and-paste “Call Me Izzy,” a star vehicle fit for the junkyard?
But what it’s actually doing is risking nothing, repeating back at you that the world is scary, that a star you like is indeed likeable, and that the theater is the land of the grim and dutiful.
She tries but fails to do it again in Call Me Izzy, a vehicle that is totally wrong for her skills.
What’s remarkable about Smart’s performance here is the way she elevates a standard issue melodrama into must-see theater.
Jean Smart is a force to be reckoned with in this sweet, funny, painful, intensely sad one-woman show, and Jamie Wax’s script will stay with you long after the curtains close.

Thanks to Jean Smart's convincing grasp of her character, Call Me Izzy soars above its seeming movie-of-the-week roots to leave us something new to ponder about cruelty, kindness, and human endurance.
Her performance is so smooth – even through rough bits – that she appears not to be acting at all.
Call Me Izzy works best as a showcase of Smart’s talents.
Today, it feels more like summertime filler than a noteworthy theatrical event.
...it takes a cunningly gifted actress to make [Izzy] believable.
It’s never wise to bet against Smart, who ultimately deserves a far better vehicle for her Main Stem comeback.
Perhaps encapsulating its central point about art and its creation and funding, Prosperous Fools is itself a hit-and-miss affair.
Smart brings the character to vivid life but she can only do so much to engage the audience when the writing falls short.
What could have been a routine feel-good story of cliches is lent a degree of depth thanks to the actress' investment in creating a full physical and emotional life.
To me, however, the entire enterprise simply feels like a case of wrong place, wrong time, and wrong theater.
Call Me Izzy takes an urgent and devastating subject and flattens it to a moralistic message, one that fits neatly on a square of toilet paper.
This new play, which veers between the predictable and the implausible, adds little to the conversation, and pales beside that canon.

Portraying the eponymous Izzy–or Isabelle per the formal preference of a long-ago teacher–the charismatic Smart earns our rapt attention throughout the play, though she cannot begin to overcome a first-person narrative that doesn’t know that person particularly well.
This highly collaborative experience is worth the price of admission.
She makes Izzy a sympathetic character despite the flaws in the play.
Smart pulls us into the conversation—not an easy task in a 1,000-seat theatre.
The main draw here is Smart, and she does not disappoint.
She is in full command of the stage, and her relationship with the audience is almost conversational, as if we are friends with her.
While the play “Call Me Izzy” is thin and meek, Jean Smart is thoroughly entertaining as the title character, and does the best given the material that she has.

cn.t: Smart delivers a magnetic performance that transcends Jamie Wax's uneven, clichéd script about an abused Louisiana trailer park housewife who finds solace in secret writing. Critics praise the star but fault the Lifetime-movie material.

sg.vl: Center Orchestra front-to-mid is the house sweet spot
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both identify center Orchestra Rows A-E as offering the most direct, immersive sightlines. The stage's setback (per TickPick) enhances Row A viewing, and Rows F-H avoid the Front Mezzanine overhang that begins at Row M. Headout lists 15 orchestra rows (A-P) totaling ~521-538 seats depending on source.

SeatPlan explicitly flags Rows F-H as 'good value seats' that avoid Front Mezzanine overhang disruption and sit at a comfortable distance from the stage. Headout and TickPick echo the value framing for this band. Pricing typically below the Row A-E premium band.

SeatPlan describes Center Front Mezz AA-BB as 'very popular' with 'excellently raked seats and expansive overhead sightlines.' No Rear Mezz overhang exists above this section. Headout prices most Center Front Mezz seats around $224. Row AA safety rail can clip the stage for shorter patrons, so Row BB is the refined pick.

SeatPlan: Left-section Front Mezz has 'more restricted sightlines of action at the corner of stage right'; Right section mirrors this toward stage left. Legroom described as 'particularly cramped' at side seats. Still elevated with no overhang above, so sightlines to center stage remain workable.

SeatPlan calls 'rows FF and GG in the Center Rear Mezzanine' the Rear Mezz sweet spot; Headout flags EE-GG as good value ('a good look at the stage without costing as much'). Row EE sits directly behind a horizontal aisle per the SeatPlan overview. Steep rake trades legroom for sightlines.

sg.vl: Side-angle obstruction into opposite stage half
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both warn that Left Rear Mezz Rows HH-NN have obstructed sightlines into stage right, and Right Rear Mezz mirrors this to stage left. Combined with the steep rake, tight legroom, and distance, these rows deliver the weakest experience in the house.

vr.q: watching Jean Smart guide us through that journey is more than worth the price of admission
